title: Remembering what was dropped
answer:
An archive of dropped text with a search tool answered questions about the past as well as summarising, in a quarter of the time.

Saving the original text matched summaries on accuracy and took less time. On this retention test, both answered every question. A current-state table alone lost details from the past.

title: The test
answer: The 119K-token narrative reading task, with twelve extra questions asked only at the end: values that were later overwritten, and small details in the text. 36 questions in all. Every approach had a 32K working budget except keep-everything, which used the full window.

title: What it showed
answer:
The archive beat summarising on time and writing, at equal correctness. Both answered 36 of 36. The archive agent took 6.1 min and wrote 14K tokens; the summariser took 26 min and wrote 121K tokens.

A running table alone cannot answer about the past. It keeps only current values, so questions about overwritten values and details went blank or wrong: 25 of 36.

The plain files agent collapsed because it has no guards. It spent its 32K budget thinking before it had finished reading and was stopped: 3 of 36. The same agent got every answer on the version without the extra questions.

title: How the archive works
answer:
When the agent drops a batch from its working context, the batch goes word for word to an archive the model can read but not change.

Recalled text counts against the 32K budget like any other tool output.

The grader voids the run if any other file holds stream data, so the archive is the only memory outside the context.

Nothing is deleted, only moved out of view. In this run the agent searched the archive 12 times. How summaries work · Why files helped on the ledger .

title: On an outside benchmark
answer:
The same ranking held on a public memory benchmark, with the archive again the cheaper of the two methods that manage context. LongMemEval_S (MIT licence), 56 of the 500 questions: 8 per question type, each with about 110K tokens of chat history. The model must answer one question about a long chat history: a fact the user mentioned once, something the assistant said, a preference, a date to work out, a fact that was later updated, or a question the history does not answer, where the right reply is to say so. Every approach ran with the same 27B model on two Intel Arc Pro B70, 65,536-token window.

The summarising approach was stopped early. Stopped after 23 questions: it was taking 16 minutes each and the comparison was already clear. On the 23 questions it did finish (the single-session user, assistant and preference questions), all three approaches can be compared directly:

3 questions only the archive got right, 2 only summarising got right, and 1 neither. That is a tie on accuracy at this sample size. The archive spent a third of the time and wrote a sixth of the tokens. A small pilot of seven questions had put summarising ahead; it did not hold up, which is what the larger run was for.

Reading the whole history in one call is still the best answer whenever it fits the window. Where the archive falls short of it: questions the history cannot answer, 1 of 8 against 4 of 8 for whole-history reading: it answers when the history does not say; and preferences, 4 of 8 against 5 of 8. Teaching the note-taker to record what was not said is the next step.

The judge: Qwen3.8-27B FP8 on the lab host, using the benchmark's official judge prompts. The benchmark's published scores use GPT-4o as judge, so these numbers are not directly comparable with published ones. The run was stopped once by the host memory guard at 52 of 56 archive trials and resumed; finished trials were kept, no GPU fault. Lab note · Per-question verdicts and scripts (2026-10-08).

Over a longer history, with questions at known distances back, the archive method was again the strongest once it had a 32K window. Past the window: what the agent still remembers .

title: 1. The server
answer:
The lab started one two-card server with its research launcher and kept it up while a client script ran. Its settings:

Window: 262,144 tokens (--max-model-len 262144), one sequence at a time.

Exact prefix cache: --prefix-cache align; the prompt is read in 832-token pieces, one cache block each, so a resumed read does the same arithmetic as a fresh one; a kept state every 13,312 tokens (--prefix-cache-retention-interval=13312). Add-on: b70-prefix-cache-exact .

Drafting on: the model’s own draft head, five tokens ahead.

Tool calling: --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3. The harness needs these; without them requests with tools are refused.

On another server, the same tool-calling flags and a window that holds the budget plus the answer allowance are what matter. How the exact cache works .

title: Past the window: what the agent still remembers
answer:
Facts, old values and standing rules across histories of up to a million tokens.

Keeper kept the most facts and rules on these long-history tests. It archives old turns, refreshes short notes and repeats standing rules outside the working agent. The proxy carries the same policy between a client and the model server.

Over a million tokens the proxy now answers 226 of 228 questions in 50 minutes, for an agent that sends its whole history and manages nothing. That is within two answers of the version built into the test harness, which answered 228 of 228 on the same stream, and just as fast. On a second million-token stream the proxy answered 214 of 222 in 48 minutes. The proxy’s earlier form answered 222 in 95 minutes.

Two more results are new. A rule that names nothing it covers stayed in the keeper’s notes and was applied 16 times out of 16; retrieval alone never found it, 0 out of 16. And two earlier claims are corrected: on a second million-token stream the keeper inside the harness answered 210 of 222, not every question, and the gain from adding retrieval on a harder stream is still measured on one seed only. The repair marathon’s two registered controls have also run — at the same medium thinking effort the summariser matched the proxy (40 of 40 clean, audit 7 of 7), and a short first cap on a thinking reply cost clean tickets and stays off. Newest: the proxy has run under an agent program that shares no code with the test harness — the lab’s own stand-alone agent scored 40 of 40 clean, audit 7 of 7, through the proxy at a 32K window in 33.3 minutes, and the same agent direct against the full 262K window scored the same in 55.0 minutes. title: Real code: the repair marathon
answer:
Everything above is a synthetic stream. The repair marathon is real code with a real test suite: more-itertools 10.7.0 with 40 injected one-token defects (a comparison turned round, plus for minus, and for or, a dropped not), worked as 44 tickets one at a time by an agent that sends one shell command per turn. Three tickets are notices carrying a standing instruction: end every changed line with # fixed, log every fix in FIXES.md, and name every recipe fix in RECIPES.txt. A ticket is fixed when its tests pass and clean when no instruction in force was broken for it. On the second seed the last ticket asks for the number and function of the seven fixes made before FIXES.md existed; nothing on disk holds that, so it tests what the method kept of the oldest work.

On the first seed every arm fixed every defect. The window dropped the recipe-name rule on every ticket where it asked for something — the notice had left its view four calls before the first recipe ticket — and kept the two instructions it could still see used. Summarising kept everything and was fastest. The proxy matched it on correctness and was a third slower: the difference was replies the model spent thinking to its 8,192-token limit and wrote nothing, which the proxy asks for again without thinking.

On the second seed the methods came apart. The proxy did everything again and answered the audit from its archive. The summariser also fixed all 40 — then lost all three instructions for the last seven tickets: its seventh summary of eleven came back as 164 characters of the next step of the work instead of a summary, and the six good ones before it, which held the notices word for word and the first tickets’ functions, were gone. A summary replaces the history, so one bad summary ends everything before it; the proxy’s notes change line by line, its rule section cannot lose a line, and the turns themselves stay in the archive. The window stuck on one hard ticket in its first two runs and was never graded; given the task’s own 55-minute limit on a third attempt it finished the queue, fixed all 40, and broke the marker and log rules on most tickets — the stalls were luck, not certainty.

Half of each arm’s time was the model thinking to its reply limit on two hard tickets. Setting the thinking effort to medium on every call the proxy forwards (arm XR4) cut its run from 47 to 29.5 minutes with the same result. That is a setting of the model, not a way of managing context, so two controls were registered and have now run. The summariser at the same medium effort, through a pass-through proxy (C32m), matched it: 40 of 40 clean, audit 7 of 7, in 20.9 minutes. With thinking kept in bounds the two methods tie on this task; what the run above showed is the proxy’s robustness to one bad summary. A 3,072-token first cap on a thinking reply (XR5) threw away about 102,000 tokens, broke the recipe-name rule on six tickets (34 of 40 clean) and was slower, so the cap stays off. Still owed: the proxy under a third-party coding agent program (the owner picks which); the lab's own stand-alone agent has now run: the same perfect score through the proxy at a 32K window in 33.3 minutes as direct against the full 262K window in 55.0 minutes.

Those two hard tickets were a property of the task, not of any method: three combinatorial *_index functions and peekable made this model think to its limit again and again, and one ticket could decide a run. The task was rebuilt without them (seed 2, the audit ticket kept). The proxy was unchanged — 40 of 40 clean, audit 7 of 7, in 20.1 minutes. The window finished the queue, fixed all 40, and kept the recipe-name rule everywhere this time (35 of 40 clean), and still answered nothing about the oldest work. What the proxy adds over the window is the same on every seed: the rules survive, and the archive answers for the distant past.

The table’s last rows close out the controls and map the proxy’s floor. The summariser’s missing third-seed row ran to full marks (40 of 40 clean, audit 7 of 7), so on every seed the proxy and the summariser now both read 40 of 40. Inside the proxy one fault had been costing speed: its note-keeping calls rendered differently from the main calls and missed the server’s prefix cache almost entirely (2–4% of their reading). Rendered like the main calls they hit 91%, and with the thinking effort set to medium on every call — which keeps the notes calls from thinking at all — the proxy ran the marathon in 15 minutes 38 seconds, the fastest run on record, on 4,549 tokens of notes. Cutting deeper at each pass (XR8) is safe but buys nothing: the pass count is set by the note-gathering threshold, not the depth. And the window curve maps the floor: the same full score at a 24K window, faster (13 minutes); at 16K the notes starve (29 passes, no note written) and exactly one ticket of forty slips — the fix worked but missed the maintainer’s mark on one line — while the archive still answers the audit of the oldest fixes 7 of 7. On the million-token stream the plain window at the largest size a dedicated card allows (200K tokens) answered 166 of 228: perfect on what still fit (current values 58 of 58, procedures 29 of 29), blind to what had slid out (the standing rule 0 of 29, old values 40 of 58).

Two rows in this table put the proxy under an agent it did not shape: the lab’s own stand-alone agent program (one shell tool, structured tool calls, thinking on, no context management of any kind), written for this comparison and sharing no code with the test harness. Through the proxy the agent worked at a 32K live window — the proxy cut 562 turns into its archive in twelve passes and kept 6,264 tokens of notes — and scored the same 40 of 40 clean with the audit answered, in 33.3 minutes. Direct against the server’s 262K window the same agent scored the same in 55.0 minutes; the difference is the history carrying every reply’s reasoning, about 215,000 tokens by the end, which the proxy strips from what it keeps. The proxy’s cost beside the window’s, on an agent the harness never shaped: two-fifths less time, nine-tenths less prompt traffic, the same score.

title: How the keeper works
answer:
Every earlier method that beat the simple baselines made the model run a routine: read a batch, fold it into a state file, drop it. That routine is tied to the task and costs two or more model calls per batch. With the keeper the agent just works. Whenever the conversation is about to outgrow the window, something outside the agent does three things:

It writes the oldest turns, word for word, to an archive on disk.

It asks the model once, with no tools, to rewrite a short NOTES block from the old notes and the turns about to go. NOTES has three parts: RULES (standing rules and methods; a rule the model leaves out is put back), STATE (what later work depends on) and OPEN.

The model also gets a search tool over the archive, and whenever questions arrive the RULES are repeated right next to them. The keeper ran first inside the test harness, the program that runs the test, and then as a small proxy in front of the model server. A later form keeps the same notes at lower cost: in-place notes .

title: How in-place notes work
answer:
Ask inside the conversation. Every ten batches, one more message is added to the end of the conversation the server has already read: write down what these turns changed. Nothing has to be read again for the notes.

Write only the changes, then check them. The model replies with the changes only, with thinking on. The test program applies them to the notes and checks them. Every mention of a tracked name must be accounted for. A worked-out value must show its working. The program redoes every sum. A reply that fails a check is asked for again.

Empty the window. Every turn in view then goes to the archive, word for word. The window starts again from the task and the notes, so nothing has to be read back.

title: An audit of the notes themselves
answer:
A perfect score does not show that the notes are right. A new tool compares every saved version of the notes with the true ledger at the point that version covers. title: Lessons from failed runs
answer:
Each of these comes from a run that went wrong. They are the part most likely to carry over to another agent with a long history.

Ask for the notes after the turns being removed, not before. In the first try the request came first, followed by about 8K tokens of the agent’s own turns. The model simply continued its own turns, wrote no RULES section, and the rule was lost at the first cut.

Give a rule a pinned place and a reminder at the point of use. With no pinned place, four methods answered 0 of 20 rule questions the way the rule required. title: Four more, from the harder stream
answer:
The harder stream broke four things. Each is now fixed in the keeper’s code.

Refusing a repeated command does not end a loop. The model sees the same conversation and the same refusal, so it sends the same command again. The fully checked keeper sent one archive search 362 times in a row at the first question set, was refused every time, and finished with 3 of 50. Now the third refusal in a row tells the model to stop and answer, and that one reply is drawn with some randomness so that it can come out different.

A search that shows only the matching sentence is blind on text that says “it”. A search for one counter’s name returned “Next on the list was nipewe33.” and never the sentence after it, which held the change. The archive search now shows each match together with the sentence that follows.

A loop can go round three commands. With repeats refused, the model circled between three different searches, and that run was stopped by hand after 11 minutes. A search sent a third time since the last batch arrived is now refused too, because the archive has not changed in between.

A reply that is asked for again must not lose what the first reply had. The first note-taking reply named the standing rule. title: Nine more, from moving the fast notes into the proxy

Getting in-place notes into the proxy took five builds. Each of the first eight comes from a run that went wrong, and each fix is now in the code with a test.

Results that only the proxy saw must not be lost. The proxy answers the model’s archive searches itself, so the agent’s history never holds them. At one set of questions the model made its eight searches and then sent an empty reply. In the next request everything it had found was gone, and six answers were never written. Searches from a turn that ended empty are now shown again in the next request.

A search tool must count one way. Search results were labelled with message numbers, while the questions speak of item numbers, the stream’s own numbering of its batches. In one run six answers about a numbered item were wrong. In the next build each result showed both numbers. The model asked for “everything before 332”, meaning item 332, and got everything before message 332, which is item 150. It trusted that search over its own correct notes: six more wrong answers, and probably a seventh. The tool now counts only in the content’s own numbers, and with that every old-value question was right (58 of 58).

A list that is cut short has to say so first. “The first 40 of 63”, with the note at the end, was read as “that is all”. A cut-off list now says so in its first line and shows the matches nearest to what was asked for.

What stays in view after a cut gets written down twice. The proxy keeps the newest exchange in view, so that a real agent can still see what it has just fetched. The model’s remark in that exchange was about the result before it, which was already in the notes. At the next note-taking call it noted those changes again, once backwards: an 84 that had been added was taken away. The request now says what that first message is, and a line about a name that the turns being noted never mention is left out.

A questioned note must never fall back to a slower, different path. When the model gave no usable answer to a question about its notes, the whole step was redone the old way, with a full rewrite. In one run that lost a change. In another the rewrite added a “rule” that only restated the task’s opening instructions. Rules are repeated at every set of questions, and at the last one the model followed that one to the letter and overwrote a file holding 25 correct answers: 14 of 39 instead of 39 of 39. Now the first reply stands, without the lines in question.

A model told to show its working will invent working. “The clerk recorded katu85 at five hundred and twenty-three” came back as 650 − 27 = 623. It adds up and it starts from the right value, so the checks passed it. Every amount in a line’s working now has to be in the text.

A safety rule can be too eager. “Leave out a note whose number is not in the text” also left out three notes that were right, or nearly right, but written in a way the checker could not follow. Their counters kept stale values. The two wrong values that were this rule’s doing cost no answer. The rule now leaves out only what the text contradicts. The server kept being stopped at the end of long runs, and it was not the run. A script that summarises the results loaded 1.7 GB of saved snapshots at once, right beside a model server with about 2 GB of memory to spare. It now loads one at a time: 50 MB.

title: The question, and how it is tested

Old value: what a counter was before it was overwritten.

Who did it: a small detail that only appeared once, in the story text.

At the end it answered final questions about the current state: 14 on the first seed, 21 on the second. Distance is counted in batches back from the question. The evidence files call each delivery an item and count distance in items.

title: Ways to manage the window
answer:
Four methods ran the distance tests, and summarising at a threshold was added later on one seed. Two variants of the archive method were added for the rule questions. The keeper ran on the rule streams. In-place notes and retrieval alone came later, on the same streams. The two together came next, and the proxy with in-place notes last.

When the window is full, the oldest turns are dropped. Nothing is kept. This is the simplest baseline, and it is lossy.

What coding agents commonly do: old tool output is replaced with a short stub and old thinking is removed, then the oldest turns go. Also lossy. Called D or P in the evidence files.

What most production agents do: when the context reaches a threshold, here 75% of the window, the model writes a summary that takes the place of the older turns. Also lossy. Called C in the evidence files.

The model reads each batch and keeps name value lines in a pinned state at the top; processed batches leave the window. How self-editing with a protected state works .

The same pinned state, and every batch that leaves the window goes word for word to a read-only archive. A recall tool searches it. How the archive works .

The archive method with one change: the pinned state may also hold permanent RULE: lines. An edit that removes or rewords one is rejected. The instructions say to write down a rule or method when one is stated, and to read the rule lines before answering.

The archive method with free-text notes in place of the name value lines. Its instructions say nothing about rules.

The agent manages nothing. Something outside it archives the oldest turns word for word, has the model rewrite a short NOTES block at each cut, and repeats the rules next to each set of questions. How the keeper works .

The same keeper with a cheaper way to keep its notes: the request rides on the conversation the server has already read, the model writes only what changed, and the window is then emptied down to the task and the notes. How in-place notes work .

title: Keeping a rule and a method
answer:
Of the methods that ran before the keeper, none kept a rule that was stated once at the start until rules had a pinned place. This 240K stream opened with the standing rule and the house method. Five later question sets each added one rule question and one method question to the usual three, 24 to 129 batches after the rule and the method were stated. One of the 14 final questions asked for a confidential counter. That makes 39 questions per run. The keeper’s 39 of 39 on the same stream is in the table at the top .

One seed at a 32K window, so each cell is a handful of questions. The first four methods ran with a 65,536-token server window and the two variants with 262,144; the live window was 32K for all. Probe analysis for this table .

The best memory method failed the rule as completely as the worst. None of the first four methods answered a single rule question the way the rule required (0 of 20), and all four missed the confidential counter at the end.

Why the archive method lost it. The model noticed the rule when it read the first batch, but its pinned state only accepts name value lines, so the rule had nowhere to stay in view. A question about a confidential counter looks like any other value question, so nothing prompted a search. It kept the house method (5/5) only because those questions name the method, which sends the model to the archive.

A pinned place for rules fixes it. With permanent RULE: lines in the pinned state and one sentence telling the model to read them before answering, all five rule questions and the confidential final question were right. It was not free on this run: four bookkeeping answers were lost (29 of the other 33 questions, against 33 of 33 without the rule lines).

Free-text notes kept the rule without being told to, but not reliably. They scored 4 of 5: one rule question got the plain answer although the rule was in view, and the confidential final question was left blank. They also kept the books worse (9 of 14 final questions).

Fetching four batches per step was not a way to go faster. At 32K it ran out of room and was stopped after 115 model calls for 21 batches. It is not scored.

title: What it shows
answer:
Managing the context from outside the agent beat every method that makes the agent manage it. The keeper answered 39/39 and 46/46 at 240K and 226/228 at 1,000,000 tokens, with fewer model calls than the methods that run a routine: 197 against 400 and 424 at 240K, and 865 against 2,170 at 1,000,000. With in-place notes it answered every question on three streams, 39/39, 46/46 and 228/228, and 210/222 on a second 1,000,000-token stream. It is also the only method here that needs no change to the agent: as a proxy in front of the model server, with in-place notes, it answered 39/39, 46/46 and 226/228 for an agent that sent its whole history and managed nothing (39/39, 44/46 and 222/228 in its earlier form).

Reading nothing twice made the keeper faster at every size tested. In-place notes took 9.9 and 10.0 minutes at 240K against 15.7 and 16.5, and 50 minutes at 1,000,000 tokens against 83. They answered 313 of 313 questions over the three streams, against 311 for the full rewrite. The proxy gained as much: 8.5 and 9.4 minutes at 240K against 17 and 18, and 50 minutes at 1,000,000 tokens against 95. In-place notes · the proxy today .

A rule that names nothing separates notes from retrieval. The keeper applied it 16 times out of 16, because the rule sits in its notes and is repeated where questions arrive. Retrieval alone applied it 0 times out of 16: no question leads a search back to such a rule. Two streams, one run each. A rule that names nothing .

A score can hide wrong notes. Notes written without thinking scored up to 39 of 39 and still held 2 to 8 wrong values in every run. Only an audit of the notes showed it. Even with every check, one misread sentence left one wrong value in the notes of a run that scored 46 of 46. The audit .

Retrieval alone did better than we expected where the rule names its counters, and was not enough at scale. There it kept up with the keeper at 240K (39/39 and 45/46) with no notes at all, then answered 56 of 70 in the last third of the 1,000,000-token stream and lost the standing rule 4 times in 29. Retrieval finds things; notes keep the rules and the current state in view. Retrieval alone .

On text that refers to things indirectly, notes and retrieval together beat either alone. On the harder stream the keeper with retrieval added answered 47 and 46 of 50. With notes only it answered 42, and retrieval alone was too slow to finish. That comparison is one seed, exploratory. On a second seed the keeper with retrieval added answered 46 of 49, and the run without it did not finish. The harder stream .

Summarising at a threshold was the slowest method and scored below dropping old turns. It answered 23/29 in 29 minutes, against 25/29 in 20 minutes for window-drop and 27/29 in 15 for archive and search. One seed.

Archive and search at 32K beat the lossy baselines on both seeds. It had the best probe score (28/30), all 35 final answers and the best total (63/65), at 15 to 16 minutes per run. On the second seed alone it scored 36/36, against 31/36 for both window-drop and compaction. The verbatim text is still there, so “who did it” questions can be answered (9/10, against 0/10 for read mode).

Compaction reported old values as current on one of two seeds. On the first seed at 32K it answered the probes well (13/15), then got only 4 of 14 final questions right: six answers were values that used to be true. On the second seed it got all 21 final questions right. Why the first seed went wrong has not been established, so this is a risk seen once, not a settled pattern. Compaction also loses “who did it” details, because those live in the tool output it stubs out (4/10 at 32K, 1/10 at 16K).

Window-drop is honest but forgets. It answered almost nothing beyond about 25 batches back in any run: 0/5 at 16K, 0/5 at 32K, and 1/6 then 0/4 even with a 48K window.

16K starves the methods that work inside the window. With the batch, the state, the instructions and room to think all inside 16K, the self-editing read mode fell to 9/30. The archive method had no room either: the harness refused to fetch the next batch 121 times and refused to fold old batches 35 times, so old values stuck (8/14 final). That was lack of room, not a fault in how recalled text was written back. At 32K neither failure appeared.

Speed did not degrade as history grew, with one exception. In the first 240K runs every method took about 4–10 minutes per 100K tokens of history in both halves of the stream. On the rule stream the archive method held at 8.5 then 7.9 minutes per 100K, while window-drop slowed from 7.9 to 12.6.

End-of-run questions alone do not separate methods. At 32K three of the four methods answered all 35 final questions while scoring from 16/30 to 28/30 on the probes. Final questions mostly ask about state that is still in view.

title: Limits
answer:
One synthetic task family, one model and one machine, with one run per cell. It is not a real agent task. The keeper’s 240K results are two streams of that one family. At 1,000,000 tokens the keeper inside the harness with in-place notes has two streams, 228 of 228 and 210 of 222. The proxy’s result with in-place notes, and both results with a full notes rewrite, are each one stream and one seed. The proxy has been run on this benchmark and on one real-code task (the repair marathon above: one model, one library, one run per cell) and under the lab’s own stand-alone agent program, not yet under a third-party coding or research agent. A plain 200K window has still not been run on the 1,000,000-token stream. The summary baseline is one seed.

The notes are not perfect. On the proxy’s million-token run five counters were wrong for a stretch, and one of them is behind one of its two missed tallies. Inside the harness, with every check, one misread sentence left one wrong value in the notes for a stretch on the second 240K stream, and one counter was wrong for a stretch on the second million-token stream. Two kinds of slip are not caught by any check yet: a change noted with the wrong sign, and a value that was set being noted as a change by the same number. Three fixes are in the code and have not been run: an open question is never moved out of view; a note is left out only when the text contradicts it; and, in the proxy’s earlier form, a reworded rule line is replaced by the original.

Retrieval alone was tested with a keyword retriever only, since there is no room for an embedding retriever beside the model on this machine, and its 1,000,000-token run is a stopped run that did not answer the final questions. The rule that names nothing was tested on two streams, one run each, and its wording about tallies was ambiguous. On the harder stream the comparison with and without retrieval is one seed, its difficulty is not calibrated, and its result is exploratory. The keeper with retrieval added has not been run at 1,000,000 tokens.

The distance results are two seeds, and the archive method has only one scored seed at 16K. The rule and method results for the methods other than the keeper are one seed. Each cell holds a handful of questions (at 25–99 batches back, 5 over two seeds and 2 on a single seed), so a difference of one or two answers is not decisive.

title: What we are trying to solve now
answer: The target is an agent that works on one task for weeks or months , with 1 to 10 million tokens of history, while its live window stays capped: 200K tokens on a dedicated GPU, or 32K–48K when the GPU is shared. The model must stay fast, accurate and on goal. The model’s own arithmetic stays exact; how the history is managed may lose information, but then the loss is measured.

title: Why the model limits the options
answer: Qwen3.8-27B is a hybrid. Most of its layers carry a running summary state forward instead of keeping one entry per past token. That state cannot have a piece cut out of the middle. The exact operations are: add new text at the end, or roll back to a saved checkpoint and read everything after it again. Cutting a block out of the middle of an ordinary attention cache is only approximate too: the later entries were computed while looking at the removed text. So an exact edit in the middle means rolling back and re-reading the tail, which the second, idle GPU could do between turns.

title: How the tests measure it
answer:
In use now: questions planted 1–4, 5–24, 25–99, 100–399 and 400 or more batches back, asking for current values, overwritten values, small details, a rule stated at the start and a method learned early.

Still to add: facts that are updated later, questions the history cannot answer, and a compaction-count axis (force a set number of compactions and plot accuracy against it).

Costs for every method: time per 100K tokens of history, tokens spent on management, peak window and cache reuse.

title: ctxkeeper: download and setup
answer:
Download ctxkeeper for a local model server. Install with Python or Docker, connect your agent, and read the measured results and limits.

Keep a long task going with ctxkeeper. This free, public-domain proxy gives your AI agent a shorter working view: current notes, opening instructions and recent turns. Older messages stay on disk, word for word, for the model to search. Install it between your agent and an existing model server.

Download stable 1.1.0: Python package (.whl) · Source archive (.tar.gz) · Release and checksums · Full guide

Tested mainly with Qwen3.8-27B on vLLM, plus a small Gemma 4 / llama.cpp check. Eleven of twelve tested coding agents fixed 39 or 40 of 40 bugs. Install and try it ; the results and limits are below.

title: What it does
answer:
Think of a desk and a filing cabinet. The model works at a small desk: the opening instructions, a page of notes and the newest messages. Everything else goes into the cabinet, unchanged. Three things keep the desk useful:

Notes, kept up to date. Every so often the model writes down only what changed: a new rule, a changed figure (with the working), a new open question. ctxkeeper checks the notes format and arithmetic it recognizes, and keeps rules already recorded in the notes. These checks do not prove that the notes are true.

Search. The model gets one extra tool, recall, that searches the cabinet. ctxkeeper answers it itself; your agent never sees that step.

Rule reminders. By default, rules recorded in the notes are repeated after new user messages. Instructions inside tool results need an optional matching rule (--recite-when). The model can still make mistakes.

The proxy changes the messages sent to the model. It manages Chat Completions requests from clients that keep sending their full history; see the client requirements . Follow the keeper step by step .

title: Does it help?
answer:
Measured with Qwen3.8-27B on two Intel Arc Pro B70 graphics cards, with a working view of 32K tokens. Each row is a real run, graded by the task’s own checker. The repair and million-token results describe the earlier released work; the two-million-token row is development work, separate from the stable download.

1.2.0 is a published prerelease; the stable download above remains 1.1.0. The 1.2.0 release gate — installing exactly as below, then the repair, long-chat and SDK checks — is running against the public download now; this page updates when it finishes. One model on one machine. The repair task in detail · The million-token runs · The two-million-token stream .

What it costs. The model writes its own notes on the same server, so nothing extra is loaded. In the million-token run about 15 of the 50 minutes went on writing notes and about 15 on reading (2.4M tokens for a 1M-token history); on the repair task notes took under a tenth of the time. A short view keeps every step fast, which is why the 200K window above took 228 minutes.

On one card. The same model on a single B70 with a 26K view fixed all 40 bugs, kept every rule and answered 7/7 in 21 minutes (two cards: 16).

title: Which model do I need?
answer:
The main task results on this page were measured on Qwen3.8-27B (FP8, served by vLLM on Intel Arc Pro B70 cards). A quick check on a second family, Gemma 4 26B (Q8, llama.cpp), passed the demo 4 of 4. Other models need checking with your task. They must call tools reliably, keep the notes format, and fit the configured working view plus their server’s overhead. The default view is 32,768 tokens, including the reply.

Let the model keep its own notes. A separate smaller keeper model, tried on a second card, was worse and slower (19 of 39 against 39/39 on the 240K test): it must read every turn afresh, while the main model re-reads its own cached view.

One card is enough: the repair task scored the same in 21 minutes (two cards: 16).

Turn the server’s prefix cache on: 91% of the notes calls’ prompt tokens came from the cache in the measured Qwen run.

With speculative decoding (MTP), keep the default in-line notes; background notes were correct but 8% slower there.

With the Qwen recipe, thinking can stay on for the agent’s turns; its notes calls disable thinking. The generic agent recipe does not set model-specific thinking options.

Not measured yet: other models’ quality through the proxy, and more than one conversation at a time. Window sizes and the speed numbers behind this advice are in Settings below.

title: Install and try stable 1.1.0
answer: You need Python 3.10 or newer with pip and venv , or Docker for the proxy, and a running model server . ctxkeeper does not download or serve a model. The proxy and demo use Python’s standard library. The commands below use a local server at http://127.0.0.1:8000 that accepts Chat Completions and tool calls, with enough context for the default 32K view.

title: Python install
answer: Replace the upstream address with your model server’s address, without /v1 . Leave this terminal running. Stop it with Ctrl-C when your agent is idle; restart the same command with the same state directory to reuse saved notes and archives. Your agent still needs to preserve and resend its full conversation.

title: Docker instead (Linux)
answer:
Build from the released source archive, then run the proxy with a persistent named volume. Linux host networking lets 127.0.0.1:8000 reach a model server running on the host. The explicit bind address keeps this example local to your machine.

Keep it running while your agent works. Ctrl-C stops the proxy; the named volume survives --rm. Run the same command again to reuse it. Docker Desktop networking differs; use a reachable host address for your setup. The demo below runs on your host and needs Python 3.10 or newer.

title: Check the connection, then run the demo
answer:
In a second terminal, check that the proxy can reach the server and list its model IDs:

The model list checks reachability; it does not test note quality. The status may be empty before the first conversation. The demo grows a conversation beyond the working view and checks a codename, a changing budget and a standing rule at the end:

The demo uses the first model returned by /v1/models; add --model your-model-id to choose another. It prints its answers and a score. Test your own workload before relying on the notes.

title: Connect your agent or app
answer:
Set its OpenAI-compatible base URL to http://127.0.0.1:18200/v1 , including /v1. Set the model to an ID from the model list above. If the client requires an API key, use unused for this local setup.

Stable 1.1.0 requires an upstream that accepts these managed calls without an API key. It does not forward the client’s Authorization header for Chat Completions and has no upstream-key option. Setting a real key in your agent will not authenticate those calls. ctxkeeper itself has no login.

Use Chat Completions (/v1/chat/completions). Other endpoints, including Responses, pass through without context management.

Send the whole conversation each time. Turn off the agent’s own history trimming and summarizing. If earlier messages disappear or change, ctxkeeper may treat it as a different conversation.

Request one reply at a time (n=1). Streaming is accepted, but the answer arrives in one piece at the end.

If your client supports custom headers, send a unique X-Ctx-Session value for each conversation and keep it on every call, including after a restart. Otherwise, ctxkeeper identifies conversations by their model and opening messages; identical openings can collide. The working view uses estimated token counts, so allow server headroom and avoid single messages or requested replies larger than the server can handle.

title: Tested with 12 coding agents
answer:
We ran twelve open-source coding agents through ctxkeeper on the same bug-fixing task: 40 bugs handed out one ticket at a time, three house rules announced along the way, then 7 questions about the earliest fixes. Each agent ran as it ships, except that its own history trimming was switched off. One run each, an hour at most, sorted by time.

Out of 40 bugs and 7 questions. The lab’s own simple agent, for comparison: 40, 39, 7 in 21 min. pi wrote its 7 answers and then deleted them, because a wrong line in its notes said the questions had never been asked (see Limits ). ForgeCode was still fixing bugs correctly when its hour ran out. OpenCode ran later on its own, with its memory capped and swap behind it, because the test machine had too little memory free for it at first. Qwen3.8-27B on the same machine, --recipe qwen, 32K working view. Running the agents found four ways their requests differed from what ctxkeeper expected, such as sending two opening instructions instead of one; version 1.0.1 handles all four. How each agent was set up · Records of every run .

title: Settings
answer:
A recipe is a set of options that were measured together; any option you give still wins.

The Qwen recipe writes its notes without thinking and keeps the prompt identical, so the server’s cache does most of the note-taking work. Both use a 32K working view, about the fastest we found:

One run each; repair times swing with how long the model thinks. Below 16K the notes no longer fit beside the newest turns, so every cut rewrote them in full; with --inplace-fit they fit, and 8K took 13 minutes and 12K 10. A bigger view is slower because the model reads more on every turn.

title: Tested before release
answer: Version 1.0.0 was installed the way you would install it and run as its instructions say. Version 1.0.1 changes only how requests are passed on, and its program files are the ones the agent test above ran. Version 1.1.0 only adds options, all off by default; with them off it sends exactly the same requests as 1.0.1, checked request by request.

title: Limits
answer:
Measured on one model family and one machine, with the model keeping its own notes. A small Gemma demo also passed; other models’ task quality has not been measured here. A separate, smaller model as the keeper did worse: LFM2.5-24B-A2B on a second card kept the house rules on 20 of 40 bugs and answered 19 of 39 on the 240K test, and it was slower, because it reads every turn afresh instead of from the main model’s cache.

The notes are written by the model, so they can be wrong. The latest development seed had one wrong counter line across 8,813 saved counter lines; an earlier run kept one wrong value for 118 notes versions. On the million-token test, one of 1,435 counter lines was wrong. The originals stay searchable, but nothing forces the model to look. In the agent test one notes line wrongly said seven questions had never been asked, and the agent deleted the answers it had already written.

No login, and everything is stored as plain text on the machine running it. The commands above bind only to the local machine. The Docker image’s own default binds to all interfaces, so keep the explicit --host 127.0.0.1 in the host-network command.

The opening instructions are always kept, so they must fit well inside the working view.
